title: Container ship sinks in Strait of Hormuz after being hit by projectile, Singapore says
description: A Singapore-flagged container ship has sunk after being struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to Singaporea
body: A Singapore-flagged container ship has sunk after being struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to Singaporean authorities.All 21 crew members of GFS Pride were evacuated and no injuries were reported after the attack on Tuesday, which caused damage and a fire, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore said.Another Singapore-flagged container vessel, GFS Giselle, sustained hull damage after being hit by a projectile on Wednesday but was able to reach a safe anchorage with all 22 crew, it added.Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a ship hit naval mines and sank while passing through what they called an "unauthorised" route in the Strait of Hormuz.The Guards released photos that appeared to show a plume of black smoke rising from a container vessel that was still afloat but down by the stern. In other photos, dozens of containers and their contents could be seen floating in the water.The Hydrographer of Pakistan warned mariners that GFS Pride had sunk 4 nautical miles (7.4km) north-west of Ras al-Sheikh Masud in Oman's Musandam Peninsula.Meanwhile, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said that two unnamed container ships had reported being struck by unknown projectiles while transiting the Strait of Hormuz between 16:40 and 17:00 GMT on Tuesday.Both vessels sustained minor damage and were able to continue their passages, it added.Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the Strait of Hormuz - which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea - and elsewhere in the Middle East since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February.At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 106 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization.The Malta-flagged container ship Safeen Prestige, which was attacked near Oman on 4 March, is the only other vessel reported to have sunk in that time.However, maritime risk management group Vanguard said on Wednesday that the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged bulk carrier Cape Dao was reported to be sinking after an unsuccessful rescue attempt, according to Reuters news agency.One seafarer was killed when the Cape Dao's bridge and accommodation area were hit by an unknown projectile as it transited through the Strait of Hormuz, north-east of Khasab, Oman, on 23 September.The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.Last month, crude exports through the waterway rose to around 80% of pre-war levels of 16 million barrels per day (bpd) on average, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler, despite an increase in attacks on shipping.

schema.headline: Container ship sinks in Strait of Hormuz after being hit by projectile, Singapore says

title: Australia’s first Michelin stars awarded to 11 restaurants
description: Australia has been awarded its first Michelin stars, with 11 restaurants in the state of South Australia receiving the distinction.Magill Estate Resta
body: Australia has been awarded its first Michelin stars, with 11 restaurants in the state of South Australia receiving the distinction.Magill Estate Restaurant in Adelaide was the only venue to receive two stars, while 10 others were awarded one star each.South Australia's government paid for incognito inspectors to visit the state, according to national broadcaster ABC, which is why no spots have been recognised in other parts of the country.The announcement comes more than a century after the Michelin Guide was first published in France and following years of unsuccessful attempts to bring it to Australia.Michelin has approached the national tourism board about bringing the guide to the country more than once, with no luck.South Australia decided to go it alone and pursued its own deal. The state government has not disclosed how much it paid, but Tourism Minister Emily Bourke defended the investment in an interview with ABC News."It is enabling us to create a tourism destination and put us on the world map," she said.The move follows Michelin's expansion into New Zealand, which became the first destination in Oceania to feature in the guide in July, agreeing to pay NZ$6.3m (£2.7m; $3.5m) over three years for its inclusion.

schema.headline: Australia’s first Michelin stars awarded to 11 restaurants

title: Fifa to offer extra £2.6bn for football development
description: Fifa is set to propose a $3.4bn (£2.6bn) increase in the amount of money it hands out for football development across the world.World football's gover
body: Fifa is set to propose a $3.4bn (£2.6bn) increase in the amount of money it hands out for football development across the world.World football's governing body wants to release the money from its reserves in a move which BBC Sport has been told would double the level of planned distribution funding for 2027-2030.The proposal will be made at a meeting of Fifa's council on Thursday and comes at a time when the organisation is under pressure following president Gianni Infantino's aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan.Infantino wanted to sell stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors but faced huge criticism for the proposal, with Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation questioning his position. Uefa and Concacaf wrote to Infantino in September calling on Fifa to pay at least $10m (£7.5m) from its cash reserves to each of the 211 member associations.In a letter then sent to Fifa's six continental confederations, Infantino - who will be standing for re-election for a fourth time in March 2027 - said he would support "the greatest level of additional funding that can responsibly be delivered".Fifa will now offer extra money from its reserves in addition to the current $2.7bn budgeted to be paid to all 211 member associations, the confederations, regional associations and certain non-Fifa affiliated associations.The breakdown is as follows:• $25m (£19m) per member association• $99m (£75m) for each of the six confederations• $8.25m (£6.3m) for each of the 13 zonal/regional associations• $1.1m (£836,000) for 100 member associations for travel and equipment solidarityThe terms of the distribution would be as follows:• One third would be allocated to women's and youth football development• One third would be allocated to infrastructure (of which there shall be equal access to women's and youth football)• One third would be allocated to projectsThe plan, including the eligibility, application, approval, disbursement, control and audit requirements, will be finalised by the Fifa council at its next meeting in December 2026.It will all be subject to approval by the 77th Fifa congress in March 2027.

schema.headline: Fifa to offer extra £2.6bn for football development

title: Davina McCall says memory loss after brain surgery was like 'advanced Alzheimer's'
description: TV presenter Davina McCall has said she experienced symptoms similar to "advanced Alzheimer's" following brain surgery.Speaking on Paloma Faith's podc
body: TV presenter Davina McCall has said she experienced symptoms similar to "advanced Alzheimer's" following brain surgery.Speaking on Paloma Faith's podcast Mad, Sad and Bad, the 58-year-old described suffering from memory loss while recovering from an operation to remove a benign brain tumour in 2024."After I'd had my brain tumour taken out, I had advanced Alzheimer's, so I couldn't remember anything," the former Big Brother host told singer and Celebrity Traitors star Faith."When I came out of the operation, I didn't know I'd had an operation," she recalled. One regular member of staff would ask McCall every day if she could remember their name. "And I'd go, 'I don't know'."The Masked Singer judge had surgery in November 2024 after a colloid cyst was found in a health check-up as part of her menopause advocacy work.In November last year she revealed she had also undergone surgery for breast cancer.She called 2025 the "hardest year" for both her and her partner.Speaking about the recovery from her brain surgery, she said: "Michael would come and visit [hospital] for two hours, and he'd go to the loo and come back, and I'd go, 'Oh my God, you're here', and I didn't know he'd been there."I couldn't watch a movie for six months because I couldn't remember what had happened in the movie 15 minutes before. [When reading] a book I couldn't remember the page before."A year ago, for the first time since the surgery, she noted, she woke up and could remember what she had done the previous day.According to the NHS, external, later stage symptoms of Alzheimer's disease include "significant problems with short and long-term memory".Alzheimer's is a progressive disease and so symptoms gradually worsen over years. After brain surgery, though, problems tend to be worst early on, then stabilise and improve over weeks to months. Some people are left with milder lasting changes.Music therapy can help people to recover from brain injuries and McCall said she believes it was ultimately singing lessons that had "healed" her.In April 2025, McCall revealed she had been told - following MRI scans - that her tumour was "not coming back".A benign tumour is not cancerous, but such cysts tend to grow slowly, according to the Brainstrust charity.Non-cancerous brain tumours are more common in people over the age of 50, and symptoms can include headaches, vision problems and drowsiness, the NHS says.McCall's surgery, known as a craniotomy, involved part of her skull being removed to take out the tumour.She has spoken about the procedure and her recovery, including on her own podcast called Begin Again.

schema.headline: Davina McCall says memory loss after brain surgery was like 'advanced Alzheimer's'

title: Wayfair among firms fined millions for misleading sales tactics
description: Wayfair is among three firms which have been fined £6m in total by the competition watchdog for illegally using misleading sales tactics – with some c
body: Wayfair is among three firms which have been fined £6m in total by the competition watchdog for illegally using misleading sales tactics – with some customers set to receive refunds.The online furniture retailer was fined £4.8m for misleading customers with time-limited offers, while online electronics seller Appliances Direct was fined £1.2m for the same practice, the Competition Markets Authority (CMA) said. Meanwhile, Gold's Gym has been fined £45,000 for not telling customers the total price of its memberships.It and Appliances Direct have been ordered to refund customers a total of £440,000. Wayfair and Appliances Direct said the CMA's fines were disproportionate.Gold's Gym has been contacted for comment.Thousands of Appliances Direct customers will receive refunds of £25 each on average while 726 Gold's Gym customers will get refunds of up to £50, according to the CMA.The watchdog said customers do not need to take any action and both companies will contact those affected customers about refunds. Appliances Direct has been told to pay refunds by 11 March, while Gold's Gym has been given a deadline of 29 March. The CMA said Wayfair, Appliances Direct, and Gold's Gym had "engaged constructively" with its investigation. They all admitted to breaking the law and agreed to settle the case early, it added.The watchdog said their co-operation reduced the firms' fines by 40%.The CMA's fines are the result of an investigation it launched last November into online pricing.A Wayfair spokeswoman said the penalty was "excessive" but that "we take the CMA's findings seriously and we chose to settle so we can continue to focus on serving our customers". Nick Glynne, chief executive of Buy it Direct, which owns Appliances Direct and several other online retailers, accepted that its practices were wrong, but said the firm should have simply been given "a rap on the knuckles" instead. Glynne said the CMA's process for calculating the fine was a "black box" and that it only settled because appealing was too expensive, accusing the watchdog of pressure tactics. "When one body is investigator, prosecutor, judge and jury, it needs an exceptional commitment to fairness, restraint and proportionality. That is not what we experienced," he added. Hayley Fletcher, senior director for consumer protection at the CMA, said: "At a time when many households are carefully managing their budgets, people shouldn't lose out because of misleading sales tactics. "Businesses must treat their customers fairly and make sure they comply with the law - or risk hefty fines."Sue Davies, head of consumer rights policy at Which?, praised the CMA's response."The refunds secured by the CMA are a much-needed win for consumers at a time when household budgets are under strain," she said.The CMA's investigation found that the three companies had misled customers in different ways.Wayfair had advertised products as if they would disappear the next day, through phrases like "Here Today, Gone Tomorrow" and countdown timers.However, the CMA said many products remained available at the same price or lower after the stated deadline, meaning the time-limited offer was false.Meanwhile, the regulator said Appliances Direct had automatically opted customers into services such as recycling old machines.Gold's Gym was fined for failing to include joining fees in the total price of gym memberships or not making its total price clear to customers, the CMA said.

schema.headline: Wayfair among firms fined millions for misleading sales tactics

title: Family pays tribute to 'warm and engaging' man killed in tiger attack
description: Image source, SuppliedImage caption, William Chapman's family has described him as "bright, warm and engaging"ByCachella SmithEmily Johnson and Alex M
body: Image source, SuppliedImage caption, William Chapman's family has described him as "bright, warm and engaging"ByCachella SmithEmily Johnson and Alex MossYorkshireUpdated 3 hours agoThe family of a man who was killed by a tiger after he entered its enclosure at a wildlife park has paid tribute, describing him as "bright, warm and engaging".William Chapman, 23, visited Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster on Saturday and was attacked after going into the animal's pen. He was pronounced dead at the scene.In a statement, his family said that he had suffered from "significant mental illness" over a number of years and had been prescribed "strong medication".His family added: "It will be for the coroner to decide what part this played in his death. We would ask everybody to respect that process."City of Doncaster Council has launched a health and safety investigation into Chapman's death.The park remains closed and a reopening date has not yet been confirmed."William was a bright, warm and engaging young man whom his family dearly loved - and William loved them back," a statement released on Tuesday evening said.The family also asked for privacy, saying "the publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time"."The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened," the statement continued."The family are hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their upmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did."Image source, Ella FordImage caption, An eyewitness took this photograph of the tiger minutes before the incidentA spokesperson for South Yorkshire Police said Chapman's family were being supported by specialist officers.An inquest is due to open into the death at Doncaster Coroner's Court on Thursday.Footage of the incident has been widely shared on social media, including on Tuesday evening by US President Donald Trump.Downing Street said people should respect the family's views on sharing footage of the incident, but declined to comment on Trump's decision to post the video.The prime minister's official spokesman said: "I think obviously the family have made their position clear. Of course, we respect that position."I'm not going to comment on the president's social media channels, he's got a press secretary who can speak to that."Also commenting on the sharing of videos on social media and Trump's posts, South Yorkshire Mayor Oliver Coppard said his office had been in contact with Chapman's family on Tuesday, with his relatives "sharing the pain and suffering it's causing them knowing that videos and pictures of his death are being shared across social media".Coppard also urged people not to speculate about the incident online."That speculation adds to the pain being endured by Mr Chapman's family," he said."Answers will come in time."Image source, Family handoutImage caption, William Chapman appeared in several TV shows as a childThe incident, which took place shortly after 13:30 BST on Saturday, led to the evacuation and ongoing closure of the park.An eyewitness described seeing Chapman wearing headphones and "pacing around" near the enclosure before he went in.Mobile phone footage, believed to be from Chapman, appears to show the inside of the enclosure as he approaches the tiger across a patch of grass.Chapman was a former pupil of the Jackie Palmer Stage School in High Wycombe."We loved watching William grow, both as a person and as a performer, during his time with us," the school said in a tribute on Tuesday."It was a privilege to be part of his journey, and he will be remembered with great fondness by everyone who had the pleasure of knowing him."Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Floral tributes have been left at the entrance to the park, near Doncaster"Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with William's family and friends during this incredibly difficult time," the statement continued.As a child, Chapman appeared in the ITV production May Contain Nuts alongside Shirley Henderson - who is best known for playing Moaning Myrtle in the Harry Potter films - and Darren Boyd.He also portrayed Edward Jenner in the BBC series True Stories.Staff at Yorkshire Wildlife Park have separately said their "thoughts and heartfelt sympathies" are with Chapman's family and confirmed the rare Amur tiger, called Altai, remained in the enclosure and would not be euthanised.Dan Swaine, the local authority's executive director of place, said the council was "deeply saddened" by the incident and sent its "deepest sympathies" to Chapman's family and those who were at the scene.Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: Family pays tribute to 'warm and engaging' man killed in tiger attack

title: US inflation rises more than expected - here's what is happening with prices
description: Inflation has risen to 3.7% in the year to September, which is a higher-than-expected increase fuelled by gasoline prices.Car fuel prices jumped by 34
body: Inflation has risen to 3.7% in the year to September, which is a higher-than-expected increase fuelled by gasoline prices.Car fuel prices jumped by 34.2% over 12 months.In September alone, they jumped by 9.1%, accounting for more than half of the increase in inflation, according to the Bureau or Labor Statistics.Overall, energy inflation was up by 20.4% over the year as prices for fuel oil, energy services and electricity climbed. Fuel oil, used in home heating, was up 74.2% over the year.Experts said the US Federal Reserve - which sets the country's interest rate - will be closely watching to see if energy costs begin to affect other areas of the economy, such as food prices, and drive inflation higher. At the moment, food inflation remains subdued. It was flat over the month of September, and was 2.5% across the year. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices, was 2.6%.

schema.headline: US inflation rises more than expected - here's what is happening with prices

title: Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Man City chairman, deleted records show
description: Andy Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Manchester City football club's chairman while mayor of Greater Manchester, it has emerged.The PM dined
body: Andy Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Manchester City football club's chairman while mayor of Greater Manchester, it has emerged.The PM dined with Khaldoon Al Mubarak at matches in 2017 and 2018 - but this was not detailed in a statement on Monday by the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) about his meetings with the club.Burnham has been under pressure to clarify his previous discussions with Man City since the club was found guilty of having "systematically" broken Premier League rules, which it will appeal.The PM, who was mayor until June, sparked widespread controversy when he said last month he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners now sold up.On Monday, the GMCA released a statement about Burnham's meetings with Man City in his role as mayor for the region for almost a decade.The statement said he had a formal meeting with Al Mubarak in October 2021 at the UK Government's Global Investment Summit, arranged by the Department for International Trade; and that he met the club chairman "informally in the stands" at a testimonial match in 2019 for former player Vincent Kompany.It also said that "in his capacity as mayor, he was a guest of Manchester City at home matches on a small number of occasions".But the statement did not specify that this referred to, external two hospitality dinners he had with the Manchester City chairman at separate matches.A previous GMCA register of declarations for Burnham, seen by the BBC, detailed a "dinner with [then-Manchester City Council leader] Richard Leese and Chair of Man City" for an Everton match at the Etihad stadium in August 2017, valued at £300 for hospitality.Below is another entry for "dinner with the Chairman at the Man City/Man Utd derby at the Etihad" in April 2018, valued at approximately £699.Burnham previously declared those dinners, alongside a £150 pair of tickets to see Ed Sheeran perform at the stadium in May 2018.But the register of declarations has since been deleted from the GMCA website, as first reported by The Sun. The BBC understands it is the authority's policy to only publish entries from the current mayoral term.BBC News has asked GMCA for more details about this policy - given its website has entries dating back to 2022, despite the current mayoral term beginning in 2024.Downing Street has defended the two dinners with Man City's chairman, saying this was hospitality received at home games, which had been declared, rather than separate meetings with the club chairman.But political pressure on Burnham to be clearer about any former discussions with Man City is continuing to mount.Tory shadow sports minister Louie French said: "Andy Burnham promised the country and House of Commons full transparency on his dealings with Manchester City."This was essential after his inappropriate intervention into football."And Reform UK's Robert Jenrick said "this saga stinks" as he accused Burnham of having apparently "concealed his extensive links to Man City's owners".Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has demanded for several days that No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club.Burnham told the Rest Is Politics podcast last week he was "happy" to do this and would "quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as Mayor of Greater Manchester". "None of it is recent, actually, in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting, actually, and that was in 2021."Asked at Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday whether anyone at the club had raised the charges they were facing with him or his team, Burnham said: "They did not raise those issues with me."With the PM continuing to face pressure on the issue, he told MPs he was happy for "everything to be set out in full", referring to the GMCA's statement as "a full statement of my key dealings with the owners of Manchester City Football Club".When asked by reporters why the statement did not refer to the two dinners, and what the difference is between "everything" and "key dealings", the PM's press secretary referred back to the GMCA statement.The list of meetings, which was published by the GMCA on Monday, did not include detail on what was discussed. The BBC has asked GMCA why the two dinners were not specifically mentioned.In September Man City - which has dominated the top flight of English football for years - was found guilty by an independent commission of breaching Premier League financial regulations.The commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than £830m into their football operations.Sanctions are yet to be announced and City, which denies any wrongdoing, has lodged an appeal against the verdict.Earlier this month, Sir Richard Leese - who was head of Manchester City Council for 25 years until 2021 - defended a decade-old deal between the council and Man City owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG).Under the partnership between the authority and the company, which is linked to the United Arab Emirates royal family, land was leased to ADUG at "below comparable rates", according to a University of Sheffield report.

schema.headline: Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Man City chairman, deleted records show

title: What surprise praise for UK economy tells us about the Budget
description: "Get your fiscal health in order," is a key message at the the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) annual meeting here in Thailand.The IMF is worried
body: "Get your fiscal health in order," is a key message at the the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) annual meeting here in Thailand.The IMF is worried about the debts of the world's biggest economies. It is doing its job as a watchdog, looking for and warning about financial vulnerabilities.In the meantime, the finance ministers of former crisis countries are boasting about how little their borrowing costs have gone up, compared to the world's biggest economies, such as the US.On three occasions in the past 24 hours, top IMF officials have praised the UK's plans to reduce its annual levels of borrowing, bucking the trend of the rest of the G7 group of countries, which includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the US.The IMF clearly seeing the UK in a different light to these major economies is very interesting. "The UK is actually one country where action to reduce debt and deficit has been taken decisively and we see the UK in that sense enjoying a bit of a better growth prospect,"  managing director Kristalina Georgieva said earlier.Her comments followed those of the IMF's chief economist Silvana Tenreyro who told me that UK borrowing reductions "stand out".

schema.headline: What surprise praise for UK economy tells us about the Budget

title: Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer
description: Image source, Reuters/DOJImage caption, A recording device (R) was wrapped in toilet paper and plugged into a TV (L)ByLaura CressTechnology reporterA
body: Image source, Reuters/DOJImage caption, A recording device (R) was wrapped in toilet paper and plugged into a TV (L)ByLaura CressTechnology reporterA Saudi national who worked for OpenAI appeared in court this week for allegedly planting a secret recording device behind a TV in one of the tech giant's meeting rooms. Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer, was arrested by the FBI and charged with using or attempting to use a device "to intercept oral communications".As yet, it is not clear what he was planning to do with the recordings. But, here's we do know so far.Help from a chatbotThe engineer asked AI to help him listen in to discussions about AI, according to an official complaint (the document filed in court).Between 17 August and 16 September, Alfozan had reportedly asked a productivity AI assistant several questions about meeting rooms and their availability.Some detailed in the complaint include "how about external partners, where would they usually meet with OpenAI at" and "can you list today's meeting in this room".The complaint also claimed that in September, Alfozan used a chatbot associated with his spouse to ask how to build and install a recording device and how to access it remotely.Alfozan had worked at the firm for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant a recorder.The room where the device was found was regularly used to hold meetings to discuss "highly confidential technical, commercial and strategic information" as well as OpenAI's "government engagements and commercial relationships", the complaint stated.Alfozan had no authority to access or be involved with meetings in the room, the complaint states.But CCTV footage recorded him near the conference room on eight separate occasions in September.Hiding in plain toilet paperOn 30 September, OpenAI staff discovered a "surreptitious audio recording device" behind a television - which had been wrapped in toilet paper. A camera was placed in the conference room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering the room and appeared to look behind the television where the device had been inserted.The complaint also stated that same day he allegedly left an unattended bag in a different room.When security personnel opened it, it was found to contain "another recording device" similar to the one discovered, as well as Alfozan's wallet and ID.In a post on X, external, OpenAI wrote it had used its own AI models to "understand the device and where it had come from".It also said: "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."Image source, Reuters/DOJImage caption, Alfozan was captured looking behind a television where a device had been insertedWho is Abdulrahman Alfozan?Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. The complaint said he was educated in the US and has been a legal permanent resident since 2020.He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI has been terminated.Alfozan's lawyer William Pernik told the BBC: "Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream."These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible and any possible reasons why."Pernik added: "In the meantime, we respectfully ask everyone to withhold judgment until full facts become known. Like every one of us, Mr Alfozan is presumed innocent, and what has been made public is an accusation, not a finding of guilt." On Tuesday, Alfozan made his initial appearance in a federal court in California. A detention hearing is scheduled on 19 October to determine whether he should remain in custody while proceedings continue.The FBI investigation is ongoing.If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£190,000) fine.

schema.headline: Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer

title: More tea? How Scotland's crops of the future could be set to change
description: Image caption, Susie Walker-Munro has been growing tea on her family farm in Angus since 2007ByScotland environment, energy and rural affairs correspo
body: Image caption, Susie Walker-Munro has been growing tea on her family farm in Angus since 2007ByScotland environment, energy and rural affairs correspondentUpdated 14 October 2026 06:02 BSTSusie Walker-Munro is one of a handful of tea growers in Scotland.She says the acidic soil creates ideal conditions for the perfect artisan brew.Costing about £40 per packet for her most expensive product, it's not going to replace the supermarket brands any time soon.Droughts, intensive downpours and diseases have created challenges for tea growers across the world as they deal with the impact of a warming planet.But some experts believe Scotland's relatively settled climate could give the tea industry here a helping hand.Image caption, Only the top few leaves are picked from each bush to make the perfect teaAs the picking season draws to a close, Susie plucks the last few leaves before proudly pouring me a small glass of her Kinnettles Gold, which is grown in a walled garden on the family farm near Forfar.She believes Scotland's latitude – sitting 57 degrees north - will always be a bar to having a year-round crop like those countries close to the equator.But she says wetter weather could help boost production."Our yields are never, never going to be high," she says."Maybe with climate change they might come up a bit, it depends if we get enough rain. Scotland could be absolutely ideal."Image source, R Gates/Getty ImagesImage caption, Workers transplanting sprouts into the ground on a farm at Haddington in 1950Susie isn't convinced tea will ever be a major crop for Scotland.But others say it could be one of a numbers of options in the future, as farmers are forced to diversify and adapt to a changing climate.Rethinking the way we farm the land might be one way to extend the range of crops produced.Countries like the Netherlands are already embracing glass houses, which could become more commonplace in Scotland. Susie says they would be a good way of growing more tea.They would also allow Scotland to produce more Mediterranean vegetables like tomatoes, cucumbers, aubergines, and even melons, according to Pete Ritchie from campaign organisation Nourish Scotland.He says an abundance of renewable energy from wind farms later in the century will make heating them relatively cheap and will cut down on air miles."We're going to be able to produce those plants with a lower carbon footprint and provide secure all-round jobs for people on brownfield sites in the cities and also on the islands and remote parts of Scotland," he says.Image caption, Scientists at the James Hutton Institute in Dundee are stress-testing plants like favaThe James Hutton Institute already has a large number of glass houses – but it is going even further by artificially creating the sort of conditions that may exist in 75 years.Climate modelling shows that Scotland can expect hotter, dryer summers and milder, wetter winters by the end of this century.The institute's new advanced plant growth centre is effectively a climate simulator.It's able to control plants' light, water and nutrient intake to test how they cope with stresses - and then select species which are likely to fare best against all that climate change can throw at them.For the past three months they have been experimenting with fava beans, which are photographed daily so scientists can monitor their progress.Dr Robert Hancock says they need to switch from breeding crops for specific environments, such as hot or dry climates, towards ones which are more generally resilient."We need to start breeding those crops now and start understanding what Scottish farming's going to look like," he says."Farmers need time to plan, we need to get those crops out to the farmers and registered."Ultimately it's about what those guys do in the fields that matters, not what we do inside a climate simulator."Image caption, Farmer David Murdoch says technology will play an even bigger role in the futureThe farmers of the 22nd Century are probably only a generation away from those starting out in the industry today.That means the current crop of young farmers will have to give the closest consideration to the businesses they hand on to their own children.And that means more precision farming, more artificial intelligence, and automation.Modern tractors and combine harvesters are so high in technology such as GPS steering that it's no longer such a leap to consider autonomous harvesting.But the chair of the Scottish Association of Young Farmers, David Murdoch, believes traditional skills will always be important."There's no point in doing it if you don't know your cattle, but embracing the technology is what keeps us competitive."Working with larger herd numbers and larger machinery to keep us producing more with less people - that's the way the world's going," says David, who farms dairy with his father at Beith in North Ayrshire.Image source, VCGImage caption, The use of glass houses to grow food is becoming more commonBut it's not just food production that will drive future changes in farming.Protecting and enhancing nature, offsetting carbon emissions, and renewable energy production are already shaping the farms of tomorrow.Health innovations may also play a growing role, with obesity drugs already showing a demand for proteins and nutrient-dense foods.Soya, flax and legumes could become a more common sight as conditions for growing them become more favourable and that desire to grow them locally continues.Prof Wayne Powell - the principal of Scotland's rural college, the SRUC - predicts that Scotland will become "the bread basket of Europe".That title is currently used to describe Ukraine, because of its abundance of fertile agricultural land and exports of crops including wheat, maize and barley."Climate change is redrawing the farming map of Europe and Scotland could become one of Europe's most important climate resilient food regions," he says."The possibility of access to cheap renewable energy could also transform the economics of Scottish farming from irrigation, refrigeration, food processing, so that we can capture more value from our land and food."Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Modern agricultural equipment is often computerised, using GPS to steerScotland's rural communities have seen major changes over the past 75 years which have resulted in far fewer people working the land.Pressure to keep food affordable for consumers while farms remain profitable will be a key driver of innovation.The changing climate and the continued destruction of our nature prevent that being a simple equation to calculate.But farmers are used to change – in the short, medium and long-term - and by the end of the century our fields will probably be as unrecognisable to today's farmers as all those who have gone before them.

schema.headline: More tea? How Scotland's crops of the future could be set to change

title: Antoine Semenyo 'froze' after alleged racist abuse at Anfield, court told
description: He said witnesses saw Mogan throw chewing gum at Semenyo, hitting the right side of his shorts.In a statement read to the court, Liverpool supporter N
body: He said witnesses saw Mogan throw chewing gum at Semenyo, hitting the right side of his shorts.In a statement read to the court, Liverpool supporter Neil Sherratt, who sits next to Mogan at matches, said he saw him approach the pitch from the disabled section of the Main Stand.Sherratt said he heard Mogan shout something along the lines of "hurry up" and saw Semenyo turn towards him.He said the footballer had a shocked expression and he believed he replied: "you what".Another Liverpool fan, Nicholas Collins, said Mogan became "very cocky and brazen" after the incident and threatened to assault police if they approached him.Mogan, who had an intermediary with him in court, told police during an interview the following day that he had shouted at Semenyo to hurry up.He claimed the footballer had called him "a cripple", which had upset him, and said he had thrown chewing gum on to the floor rather than at Semenyo.Jones told the court the prosecution's case was that Mogan had lied during his police interview.Semenyo is expected to give evidence over a videolink.Mogan, of Templehill Close, Dovecot, denies racially aggravated behaviour.The trial continues.

title: Pope's cancer diagnosis leaves Catholics questioning what comes next
description: Certainly, given the dangers surrounding air travel soon after lung surgery, and the high altitude of some of the stops involved, a November trip to S
body: Certainly, given the dangers surrounding air travel soon after lung surgery, and the high altitude of some of the stops involved, a November trip to South America – including to Peru, the country Pope Leo called home for more than 20 years – may be in doubt.His predecessor, Francis, once wrote that he had started his papacy thinking he might only have a few years in the role, having already suffered health complications throughout his life.As such, it was clear that he was intent on making waves quickly and implementing what some saw as fairly radical change in the Church at a swift pace.While Pope Leo's papacy has undoubtedly started in what appears to be a comparatively measured way, he has still grown quickly into being a powerful, uncompromising and compassionate moral voice on the world stage.His messaging in opposition to war, in support of the dignity of migrants and on the dangers of AI in particular has stood out in its clarity.To some extent, he has already done what many Catholics had feared was barely possible, in starting to bring closer together different factions of a Church that had seemed somewhat divided.Noticeably, both progressive and traditionalist followers often talking of him as a voice that reflects their own.But even after successful surgery, and with no details yet about what happens now, speculation has already begun as to whether a cancer diagnosis will mean an evident shift in Pope Leo's pace in implementing changes he sees as necessary.On the other hand any dramatic moves, such as on doctrine, would certainly feel out of character for a Pope who for nearly a year and a half has shown himself to be measured, thoughtful and discerning, as well as having a focus on stability.

schema.headline: Pope's cancer diagnosis leaves Catholics questioning what comes next

title: Are the European 2027 Women's World Cup play-offs working?
description: One of the main reasons for Tuesday night's results was that only one team from the league phase groups received automatic qualification.The Netherlan
body: One of the main reasons for Tuesday night's results was that only one team from the league phase groups received automatic qualification.The Netherlands, 2017 European champions, finished second in their group behind France, ranked sixth in the world. They went on to beat Hungary 11-0 on aggregate.Norway, World Cup winners in 1995 and six-time European finalists, lost out to giants Germany in their group and ended up beating Romania 8-0.Other League A fallouts Sweden and the Republic of Ireland thrashed their opponents 15-0 and 12-0 respectively. So it was no surprise when back-to-back European champions England, who were drawn in the same group as world champions Spain, went on to record another heavy victory against much weaker opposition from League C in their play-off."Of course we wanted to qualify straight away, that's not the case," said England manager Wiegman when asked about the qualification process again on Tuesday."For us now, the facts are that we are in the play-offs, we have played Greece, now we're through, and now we're going to play Ukraine. That's what my focus is on."Uefa will review how things are set up and see whether they think it works or it should be better, or different. I don't think it's my place now to review that."The Lionesses still have another two-legged tie against Ukraine to play, with the first leg taking place away from home on 1 December and the return fixture at Wembley Stadium on 5 December.Ukraine are a side who England beat twice in the league phase by an aggregate score of 9-1.It seems absurd that they should have to beat the same team on at least three occasions as part of their qualification process.England have won seven of their last eight qualifying matches, scoring 21 goals, conceding just six times, and their only defeat was away from home against world champions Spain.They came runners-up in League A3 only on their head-to-head record with the best team in the world - they even beat Spain 1-0 at Wembley.England's overall tally of 15 points in the league phase was beaten by just three other teams - Germany, Switzerland and Hungary. Switzerland and Hungary were also in qualifying groups in League B and League C that did not include a single team from the world's top 45 ranked nations.In contrast England, who were seeded in League A, had Iceland - ranked 13th - as a tricky opponent, and world number one Spain in their four-team group.When qualifying for the 2023 Women's World Cup, England beat Latvia on two occasions, winning 20-0 and 10-0 .That tournament saw an increase from 24 to 32 teams and while qualification was still one-sided, the showpiece in Australia and New Zealand was a different story.England were tested against debutants Haiti in the group stages, narrowly winning 1-0, and by Colombia in their quarter-final, despite the South American side failing to qualify for the previous tournament.The level of competition was growing and it was evident even more so across Europe with England failing to qualify for the 2024 Olympic Games on behalf of Team GB after finishing second to the Netherlands in their Nations League group.A draw with Portugal and defeat by Belgium were suffered by England the following year, while they were forced to overcome two penalty shootouts in Euro 2025.There is no denying that England's competition has improved but they were still dealt a rough hand in this year's World Cup qualifying campaign.Following their costly 4-0 defeat by Spain in June, Wiegman said: "The competition in Europe is really high."What I'm disappointed about is that we win five games, we have 15 points and we're in a group with the world champions and then you can't qualify."I'm happy with the performances but not the result of us having to go into the play-offs. That's just the way it is."What is frustrating for England is that while they picked up a routine win over Greece and now prepare to face an opponent they have already played twice in 2026, their potential World Cup rivals are getting to play matches against top-tier teams.Two of the tournament favourites Germany and Japan met in a friendly match on Tuesday night; Brazil and Argentina played out a 2-2 draw and four-time world champions USA played Spain twice in five days in a mouth-watering meeting.Fifa has announced that the 2031 Women's World Cup will be expanded from 32 to 48 teams and it is too early to know if that is the right decision.But while larger scorelines remain, it is clear it is more a direct result of a European qualification process that doesn't benefit the majority.

schema.headline: Are the European 2027 Women's World Cup play-offs working?
